Draft: draft.md (British English). Source: source.md (English). No translation is involved, and the quotations are in the source language. So every finding below is a source-support finding. There are no translation findings.

## Claim accounting

| # | Draft passage | Source passage | What differs | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Title: "Fenwick's bench schedule shows which instruments await parts" | "The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026 … says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts." / "The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience" / "postponed adding the backlog" | Attribution: the summary's report becomes an unattributed fact. Time: past, during the trial, becomes a general present. Subject: staff could see, which becomes the schedule shows. | **Finding 1** |
| 2 | Standfirst: "trialled Benchline's shared bench schedule for six weeks" | "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule." / "The team chose Benchline" / "trial summary, dated 23 February 2026" | Duration: "began a six-week trial" gives the planned length. "trialled … for six weeks" says the trial actually ran that long. | **Finding 2** |
| 3 | Standfirst: "Workshop manager Priya Vale explains what the team had to agree first" | Q: "What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?" Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant." | "first" matches "before the schedule was useful". "explains" (present tense) is the usual convention for reported interview answers. | Supported |
| 4 | Standfirst: "and what would get an extra week next time" | Q: "Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?" Vale: "I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog." / "postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions" | Time: "next time" puts the extra week in a future repeat of the process. The source leaves open whether Vale meant a repeat or the backlog addition that is still pending. | **Finding 3** |
| 5 | "Jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work previously appeared on separate paper sheets at Fenwick Instrument Repairs" | "Previously, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets." | None. | Supported |
| 6 | "a brass and woodwind repair workshop" | "Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments." / "the workshop" / "repair duration" | "services" becomes "repair". The firm's name and "repair duration" support repair work. Neither passage states exclusivity, so the scope is the same. | Supported |
| 7 | "In January 2026 its team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule." | "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule." | None. "its" is third person singular, has no natural gender and refers to the workshop. | Supported |
| 8 | "The workshop's own summary and its manager's email answers show what the trial did and did not establish." | "The workshop's trial summary …" / "email interview … between Benchline's case writer and workshop manager Priya Vale" / "The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience, not a measured improvement…" / "It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction." | This is the author framing the evidence, and it rests on the material. "its" refers to the workshop (singular, no natural gender). | Supported |
| 9 | H2: "The workshop set the rules and Benchline configured them" | "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices" | "rules" covers the status definitions and who updates them. "them" is third person plural with no gender and refers to those rules. | Supported |
| 10 | "The team chose Benchline after checking that it could tell those two statuses apart." | "The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses." | "tell apart" is the same as "distinguish". "two" is settled by the two statuses named earlier. "it" refers to Benchline (singular, no gender). | Supported |
| 11 | "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them; Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session." | Same wording in the source. | None. | Supported |
| 12 | "Collection arrangements were still discussed with customers by telephone." | "The team continued to use telephone calls to discuss collection arrangements with customers." | "still" matches "continued". The passive drops the subject "the team", but no other party could be meant. Neither passage claims telephone was the only channel. | Supported |
| 13 | "Asked what the team had to settle before the schedule was useful, workshop manager Priya Vale replied:" | Q: "What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?" | The question is paraphrased accurately. "replied" fits an email answer and adds no spoken exchange. | Supported |
| 14 | Quotation: "‘We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.’" | Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench." | Word for word, with British quotation marks. "We" (first person plural) is Vale's own. "it" refers to the part. The source records that Vale approved publication. | Supported |
| 15 | H2: "Fenwick's own record leaves repair speed unmeasured" | "It does not measure repair duration" / "not a measured improvement in repair speed" | "repair speed" is the material's own term. "record" refers to the trial summary. | Supported |
| 16 | "The summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule and says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction." | Same wording in the source. | None. The attribution to the summary is kept. | Supported |
| 17 | "Vale approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions." | "The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions." / "workshop manager Priya Vale" | "The manager" is identified as Vale by the material. "its" refers to the team, as in the source (singular, no gender). | Supported |
| 18 | H2: "The manager weighs the decision" | The interview answers and the approval of continued use | The heading frames the Q&A that follows. It asserts no event, emotion or undecided state as fact, and the decision's outcome is stated just above. | Supported (framing) |
| 19 | "Would Vale make the same choice again, and what would change?" | Q: "Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?" | The question is paraphrased in the third person and presented as a question, not an assertion. No claim differs. | Supported |
| 20 | Quotation: "‘I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.’" | Vale: "I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog." | Word for word. The preceding question makes Vale the speaker. "I" (first person singular) and "it" (the schedule) are hers. The hedging "would" is kept. | Supported |
| 21 | "A manager weighing a shared schedule might start with the question Fenwick had to answer: what does ‘ready for work’ mean on your benches?" | "We had to agree what ready for work meant." / "not … a recommendation for every workshop" | This is the author's own hedged suggestion ("might"), resting on the supported fact that Fenwick had to settle this question. It does not claim the schedule is right for every workshop. "your" addresses the reader. | Supported (author reflection) |
| 22 | Pronouns for Vale | The material gives no pronoun or gender for Vale. | The draft uses no third-person pronoun for Vale anywhere, so it asserts no natural gender. | Supported |

## Findings (source support)

### Finding 1: the title turns the summary's reported past observation into an unattributed present fact

- **Draft:** "Fenwick's bench schedule shows which instruments await parts"
- **Source:** "It [the workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026] says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts." / "The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience" / "The manager … postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions."
- **Difference:** The source reports what the summary says staff could see during the trial. The title states, without attribution and in the present tense, that the schedule shows which of Fenwick's instruments await parts.
- **Case where the draft fails and the source holds:** The backlog has not been added to the schedule, which the material states. At publication, backlog instruments that are waiting for parts do not appear in it, so the schedule does not show which of Fenwick's instruments await parts. The summary's report of what staff could see among the jobs entered during the trial is still true. No supplied statement rules this case out.
- **Smallest supported repair:** Attribute the claim and keep the past tense, for example "Fenwick's trial summary: staff could see which instruments awaited parts".

### Finding 2: "trialled … for six weeks" turns the trial's planned length into its actual length

- **Draft (standfirst):** "Fenwick Instrument Repairs trialled Benchline's shared bench schedule for six weeks."
- **Source:** "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule." / "The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026"
- **Difference:** The source says a six-week trial began. The draft says the trial ran for six weeks. Duration is a circumstantial claim.
- **Case where the draft fails and the source holds:** The trial began on 20 January 2026, the summary was written on 23 February, and the manager approved continued use at that point. That is under five weeks, so the trial never ran for a full six weeks. No supplied statement rules this case out.
- **Smallest supported repair:** "Fenwick Instrument Repairs began a six-week trial of Benchline's shared bench schedule in January 2026." The body sentence in item 7 is already correct.

### Finding 3: "next time" settles a time frame that Vale's answer leaves open

- **Draft (standfirst):** "…and what would get an extra week next time."
- **Source:** Q: "Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?" Vale: "I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog." Also: "postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions."
- **Difference:** The draft places the extra week in a future repetition. Vale's answer can equally refer to the backlog addition that is still pending at Fenwick. The source does not settle which she meant.
- **Case where the draft fails and the source holds:** Vale means that, before the pending backlog addition, she would allow another week to check the status names, and no further deployment is in view. Her quoted words stay true, and "next time" is wrong. No supplied statement rules this case out.
- **Smallest supported repair:** Delete "next time": "…and what would get an extra week." Avoid adding a gendered pronoun for Vale, since the material supplies none.

## Translation findings

None. The source and the draft are both English, and the quotations are given word for word.

## Completion status

Complete. Every factual and attributed claim in the title, standfirst, headings, body and closing has been accounted for. Three source-support findings (1–3) are unresolved in the draft, and each has a proposed repair. There are no translation findings.

Claims section of the base contract:

"""
## Claims

Every claim is supported by the text or its material, with exact attribution and proportionate strength. Preserve the state of knowledge: what is unknown or unclaimed is not thereby known not to have happened. Keep uncertainty where it exists and certainty where it is warranted. A fact, quotation, source, scene, personal experience or opinion attributed to somebody is never invented to complete a form. Name the actual source of an attributed claim rather than invoking unnamed studies or experts.

Circumstantial detail is a claim too: duration, manner, motive, absence and background all need support. So does an evaluative characterisation: calling a count high, low or modest needs a comparison, target, capacity or speaker assessment. Otherwise give the count with its exclusions, without that assessment.

A sequence or correlation establishes no cause. A causal verb such as *shortened* needs causal support; a causal hedge such as *suggests that it shortened* still adds that attribution. This boundary holds in the title, summary, headings and body alike. Preserve chronology, scope and qualifications wherever a claim appears.

A stated length constrains the use of material and is never a licence to add to it. When the material is insufficient, deliver the length the material supports and name what further material would close the gap. A supplied publication limit is binding; meeting it cannot justify invention or loss of a qualification that changes a claim.
"""

Quotation guidance:

"""
# Quoting speech

Read this before putting quotation marks around anything somebody said. It applies to interview transcripts, recorded remarks, meeting notes, and any other material where the words are a person's rather than a document's.

Speech is not written prose, and a transcript quoted raw reads as carelessness towards the speaker rather than fidelity to them. So a spoken quotation may be repaired — cautiously, within a boundary that is easier to state than to feel your way to.

When translating permitted quotations, preserve meaning, stance, certainty and distinctive voice in idiomatic target-language speech, not source-language syntax. The restrictions below protect that substance; they do not require word-for-word translation. Make an implicit referent explicit only when the supplied context settles it. Where the meaning remains ambiguous, paraphrase what is established rather than inventing a fluent interpretation.

## What may be repaired

The syntax of speech: a sentence abandoned halfway and restarted, a subject left behind by its verb, a clause that never closes. Fillers — *you know*, *sort of*, *liksom*, *alltså* — where they carry nothing. Repetition that is the speaker searching for a word rather than insisting on one. False starts, and the small disfluencies a person does not hear themselves make.

That is the whole list. Everything on it is noise the speaker did not intend to produce, and removing it leaves what they meant to say.

## What may not

**Meaning.** Not narrowed, not widened, not sharpened. A speaker who said *most of them* has not said *all of them*, and one who said *we looked at it* has not said *we rejected it*.

**Stance.** Approval stays approval, reluctance stays reluctance, and a speaker who was careful not to blame anybody is not made to blame somebody by a tidier sentence.

**Certainty.** *I think*, *probably*, *as far as I know*, and *we are not sure yet* are the claim, not padding on it. Removing a hedge manufactures a confidence the speaker did not have; adding one takes away a confidence they did.

**Distinctive wording.** Where the speaker reached for an unusual word, an image, a piece of slang, or a phrasing that is theirs, it stays. Smoothing it into the register of the surrounding article is the most tempting of these failures and the one a reader can least detect.

**A self-correction.** Where a speaker gives a number or a fact and then corrects it, the correction is what they said. Quoting the first version is a misquotation; quoting a version that never existed — the correction with the correcting away — is worse.

**Anything additive.** Add no new meaning: no fact, stance, certainty, name, figure or connection that the speaker did not supply. A permitted repair or translation may change words only to render that same meaning.

## When to paraphrase instead

Where fidelity is uncertain, paraphrase. A paraphrase that attributes carefully — *she said the change had taken about a year, and that she was not sure it would hold* — is accurate, useful, and honest about what the material supports. A fluent direct quotation assembled out of a fragmentary answer is none of those things, however good it sounds.

The cases that should turn into paraphrase: material that is a summary of what somebody said rather than their words; a transcript too broken to repair inside the boundary above; several remarks that would have to be welded together to make one sentence; and any moment where you find yourself choosing between two readings of what the speaker meant.

Signal what the material actually is. Where the source is notes rather than a recording, the text says what the person said and does not pretend to their exact wording.

## What stays outside this

Whether the speaker approves the quotation. Quote approval is a human arrangement between the writer and the person quoted, and nothing here verifies it or stands in for it. A draft may say a quotation is unapproved; it may not treat the absence of approval as a problem it has solved.
"""

Task:

Compare the complete draft, including headings and implications, with the supplied material. For every factual and attributed claim, record the draft passage beside the source passage it rests on, quoted in the source’s own words and language, and carry over grammatical modifiers and qualifications that apply across clauses. Account separately for the person, number and natural-gender information conveyed by pronouns; identifying their referent does not establish those features. Distinguish natural-gender assertions from purely grammatical gender. For each pair, state what differs: the thing named or measured, the subject, scope, time, modality, certainty, or whose knowledge or assertion it is. A term carried into another language names the same thing only where nothing in this context could fall under one term and not the other. Where the two differ, test both directions: name a concrete case, compatible with the supplied material, in which one statement holds and the other fails. The case need only be compatible with the supplied material; the material need not describe it or make it likely. Set a case aside only by quoting a supplied statement that excludes it. If a case stands, that is a finding, however natural or cautious the draft’s wording; if you can name none, it is not. A claim with no source passage is a finding unless it is the author’s own argument, reflection or advocacy resting on supported material. Read such a passage as an ordinary reader would in its context, and test the facts, events, experiences and views it presents as given, not the reasoning or transition itself. Read every statement for what it does in its context and preserve who stands behind it: a valuation, a rhetorical generalisation or a position the brief gives as the commissioning party’s own is supported as that party’s standpoint wherever the brief carries it, and needs no external evidence to be expressed as theirs. That the brief establishes who asserts something establishes nothing about whether it is so. A figure, an event, a technical effect or a claim about an actual population stays a factual claim whoever supplied it, and calling one an opinion supports nothing. Where the line between a standpoint and a factual assertion is genuinely unsettled, report that passage as the brief’s own unevidenced statement or as an editorial question rather than as a defect with a repair. A finding is a defect in the draft rather than a preference about it; do not report what is defensible as written. For each finding, show the support that is missing or changed and propose the smallest supported repair. Preserve supported claims, warranted certainty, voice and editorial choices. Judge source support. A meaning changed in crossing languages outside quoted speech is a source-support finding. For translated quotations, separately check that the same meaning and distinctive voice are expressed in idiomatic target-language speech. Identify a concrete obstruction to that reading, not merely a preferred synonym; clarify an implicit referent only where the supplied context settles it. General editorial and mechanical review are outside this comparison. Distinguish source-support findings from translation findings. Write the complete claim accounting and findings to the report path, ending with completion status and any unresolved findings. Reply in at most 150 words with completion status and the report path. Where you cannot write that file, say in your reply that the file could not be written and why, and give the complete report there instead, ending it the same way; the 150-word limit does not apply to that reply.

# Claim accounting: Fenwick customer case (report 2)

Draft: draft.md (British English). Source: source.md (English). No quotation is translated, so there are no translation findings. The byline "By Thomas" is outside the comparison, as instructed.

## A. Claim-by-claim accounting

### A1. Title
Draft: "Fenwick reports staff could see instruments awaiting parts"
Source: "The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, … It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts."
Difference: "Fenwick reports" stands for the workshop's own summary. The attribution is the same, since the summary is the workshop's. "could see instruments awaiting parts" is a slightly shorter form of "could see which instruments were waiting for parts". In the context of a schedule, an ordinary reader takes both to mean identifying status. The tense is the same (past). The title adds no causal verb and no measure. Setting aside the ambiguity of physically seeing the instruments, I can name no case where one statement holds and the other fails. No finding.

### A2. Standfirst, sentence 1
Draft: "Fenwick Instrument Repairs put Benchline's shared bench schedule on a six-week trial."
Source: "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule." / "The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses." / "The workshop defined the statuses … Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session."
Difference: the source's subject is "the workshop team"; the draft's is the business. The workshop is the team's, so this is the same party. "Benchline's" schedule is inferred, and the source settles the inference: Benchline configured the workshop's status choices and trained staff on it. "put … on a six-week trial" names the kind of trial and does not claim the trial was completed, so it matches "began a six-week trial". No finding.

### A3. Standfirst, sentence 2
Draft: "Workshop manager Priya Vale explains what the team had to agree first, and which step would get an extra week."
Source: "workshop manager Priya Vale" / Question: "What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?" Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant." / Vale: "I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog."
Difference: "first" renders "before the schedule was useful", which is acceptable. "would get an extra week" keeps the conditional "I would allow another week". The step is "check the status names". Certainty and modality are preserved. "explains" (present) fits an email interview, and the draft implies no speech or scene. No finding.

### A4. Paragraph 1, sentence 1
Draft: "Jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work previously appeared on separate paper sheets at Fenwick Instrument Repairs, a brass and woodwind repair workshop."
Source: "Previously, jobs awaiting parts and jobs ready for work appeared on separate paper sheets." / "Fenwick Instrument Repairs services brass and woodwind instruments."
Difference: "services" becomes "repair workshop". The business name ("Instrument Repairs"), "the workshop" and "repair duration" in the source support "repair workshop". "a brass and woodwind repair workshop" suggests a specialism no more strongly than "services brass and woodwind instruments" does. Neither statement excludes other instruments. No finding.

### A5. Paragraph 1, sentence 2
Draft: "In January 2026 its team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule."
Source: "In January 2026 the workshop team began a six-week trial of a shared bench schedule."
Difference: none. "its" is third person, singular and neuter, and refers to the workshop. No finding.

### A6. Paragraph 1, sentence 3
Draft: "The workshop's own summary and its manager's email answers show what the trial did and did not establish."
Source: "The interview took place by email." / "The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience, not a measured improvement in repair speed or a recommendation for every workshop."
Difference: this is the author's framing of the source material, and it is supported. "its manager" refers to the workshop's manager, Vale, whom the source names as "workshop manager Priya Vale". No finding.

### A7. Heading 1
Draft: "The workshop set the rules and Benchline configured them"
Source: "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices"
Difference: "the rules" summarises "the statuses" and "who would update them", and "configured them" renders "configured those choices". The scope and the agents are the same. No finding.

### A8. Section 1, sentence 1
Draft: "The team chose Benchline after checking that it could tell those two statuses apart."
Source: "The team chose Benchline after checking that it could distinguish these statuses."
Difference: "those two statuses" refers back to awaiting parts and ready for work, which are the "these statuses" of the source. "it" is neuter and singular and refers to Benchline, the same referent the source's "it" has. No finding.

### A9. Section 1, sentence 2
Draft: "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them; Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session."
Source: "The workshop defined the statuses and decided who would update them. Benchline configured those choices and trained four staff in one online session."
Difference: none. "them" is plural and refers to the statuses, as in the source. No finding.

### A10. Section 1, sentence 3
Draft: "Collection arrangements were still discussed with customers by telephone."
Source: "The team continued to use telephone calls to discuss collection arrangements with customers."
Difference: the passive voice omits the agent ("the team"). "still" renders "continued". Neither statement claims the telephone was the only channel. The draft's context, a workshop team, leaves the agent unchanged in effect. No finding.

### A11. Quotation lead-in and quotation 1
Draft: "Asked what the team had to settle before the schedule was useful, workshop manager Priya Vale replied: 'We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench.'"
Source: Question: "What did the team have to settle before the schedule was useful?" Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant. A part being in the building did not always mean that it had reached the right bench."
Difference: the question is rendered faithfully in indirect form. The quotation is verbatim, with British single quotation marks. "replied" is neutral and adds no spoken exchange, expression or emotion. "We" is first person plural, as the speaker wrote it. Publication was approved: "Publication of the extract was approved by Vale." No finding.

### A12. Heading 2
Draft: "Fenwick's own record leaves repair speed unmeasured"
Source: "It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction." / "not a measured improvement in repair speed"
Difference: "repair speed" and "repair duration" measure the same thing here, and the source itself uses "repair speed". The heading limits the claim to the record, so it does not claim repair speed went unmeasured everywhere. No finding.

### A13. Section 2, sentences 1–2
Draft: "The summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule and says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction."
Source: "The workshop's trial summary, dated 23 February 2026, records 38 jobs entered in the schedule. It says staff could see which instruments were waiting for parts. It does not measure repair duration, revenue or customer satisfaction."
Difference: none. The count carries no evaluative characterisation. No finding.

### A14. Section 2, sentence 3
Draft: "Vale approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions."
Source: "The manager approved continued use for new jobs but postponed adding the backlog until the team had reviewed its status definitions."
Difference: the draft names "The manager" as Vale. The candidate case is a different manager making the approval before Vale was in post. I set it aside on these supplied statements: the brief asks "what its manager would approach differently", the material says "The manager approved…", and the only manager the material names is "workshop manager Priya Vale". The package therefore describes a single manager. The draft, like the source, leaves the approval undated and does not attribute it to the summary. "its" is neuter and refers to the team or workshop. No finding.

### A15. Heading 3
Draft: "The manager weighs the decision"
Source: Question: "Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?" Vale: "I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog."
Difference: "weighs" can be read as deliberating. In context, though, the section reports her retrospective assessment of the choice she was asked to reconsider, which is what the question asked her to do. The heading attributes no expression or emotional reaction. Defensible as written. No finding.

### A16. Section 3, question
Draft: "Would Vale make the same choice again, and what would change?"
Source: Question: "Would you make the same choice again, and what would you change?"
Difference: the subject of the second clause changes. The source asks what Vale would change, which is her own action. The draft asks what would change, which is impersonal and could include circumstances outside her control. See finding F1.

### A17. Quotation 2
Draft: "'I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog.'"
Source: Vale: "I would use it again for new jobs. I would allow another week to check the status names before adding the backlog."
Difference: verbatim. Attribution to Vale is clear from the preceding question. "I" is first person singular, as written. "it" refers to the schedule or Benchline, as in the source. The conditional "would" and the scope "for new jobs" are kept. No finding.

### A18. Closing sentence
Draft: "A manager weighing a shared schedule might start with the question Fenwick had to answer: what does 'ready for work' mean on your benches?"
Source: Vale: "We had to agree what ready for work meant." / "The summary and interview establish the team's reported experience, not … a recommendation for every workshop."
Difference: this is the author's hedged reflection ("might start with"), and it rests on a supported fact: Fenwick had to agree what "ready for work" meant. It does not present the trial or Vale as recommending the schedule to every workshop, and it recommends no product. "your" is second person and addresses the reader. No factual claim goes beyond the source. No finding.
